title: The Nettle Tree Bishop
translation: Ryōgaku, the bishop, was the older brother of Kinyo, a nobleman of the second rank, and he had a terrible temper. There was a big nettle tree next to his lodgings, so people called him "the Nettle Tree Bishop". He decided that wouldn't do and had the tree cut down.

The stump was still there, so people called him "the Stump Bishop". Now he was really angry. He had the stump dug up and thrown away, and that left a big ditch. So people called him "the Ditch Bishop".
original: {公世|きんよ}の{二位|にゐ}の{兄|せうと}に、{良覚僧正|りやうがくそうじやう}と{聞|きこ}えしは{極|きは}めて{腹|はら}{悪|あ}しき{人|ひと}なりけり。
{坊|ばう}の{傍|かたはら}に{大|おほ}きなる{榎|えのき}ありければ、{人|ひと}、「{榎|えのき}の{僧正|そうじやう}」とぞいひける。
この{名|な}{然|しか}るべからずとて、かの{木|き}を{切|き}られにけり。
その{根|ね}のありければ、「{切杭|きりくひ}の{僧正|そうじやう}」といひけり。
{愈|いよいよ}{腹立|はらだ}ちて、{切杭|きりくひ}を{掘|ほ}りすてたりければ、その{跡|あと}{大|おほ}きなる{堀|ほり}にてありければ、「{堀池|ほりいけ}の{僧正|そうじやう}」とぞいひける。
literal: The man known as Bishop Ryōgaku, older brother of Kinyo of the Second Rank, was an extremely bad-tempered person.
Since there was a big nettle tree beside his lodging, people called him 'the Nettle Tree Bishop'.
Saying this name was not proper, he had that tree cut down.
Since its root remained, they called him 'the Stump Bishop'.
He got angrier still and had the stump dug up and thrown away, and since the spot became a big ditch, they called him 'the Ditch-Pond Bishop'.

notes.text: Fujiwara no Kinyo (died 1301), a courtier of the second rank and a poet.
{兄|せうと}: 'brother'. Here, the older brother. Not modern あに, though the kanji is the same.
{僧正|そうじやう}: the highest rank in the priesthood. The translation says 'bishop'.
{腹|はら}{悪|あ}し: 'bad-tempered'. The belly ({腹|はら}) is where anger lives; modern {腹|はら}が{立|た}つ 'to get angry' uses the same image, and so does {腹立|はらだ}ちて later in this section.
{榎|えのき}: the Chinese nettle tree (Celtis), a large shade tree, often planted along roads.
れ: the respectful る, for the bishop. He did not cut it himself; he had it cut.
{堀|ほり}: a ditch or moat, often filled with water, so 'ditch-pond'. Each attempt to get rid of the name gives people a new one. ぞ … ける closes the story, and Kenkō adds nothing.
